analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing and monopolization.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, federal antitrust laws have generally not applied to insurance companies, allowing insurers to fix prices and divide up markets without facing lawsuits. This bill would strip that exemption for the most serious offenses: price fixing, dividing territories or customers among competitors, forcing customers to buy one product to get another, and monopolizing markets. It would keep the exemption for benign cooperation like sharing historical loss data and actuarial work.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses who buy insurance would benefit if competition lowered prices and broadened choices, and honest insurers competing on price would gain against rivals that coordinate instead.

how_it_helps.text: Insurance companies could be sued under federal antitrust law for price fixing, allocating markets, unlawful tying, and monopolization, ending a shield they have held since the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945.

The bill preserves the exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data and performing actuarial services, so the routine information-sharing that helps insurers price risk accurately would remain legal.
The bill would take effect one year after enactment, giving insurers time to adjust.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers that currently coordinate pricing or divide markets would face antitrust liability, and could see margins fall if competition compressed prices.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of the McCarran-Ferguson exemption argue insurers need to share claims data and rate information to price risks accurately, and that federal antitrust enforcement could chill legitimate cooperation; the bill tries to address this by carving out loss-data sharing and actuarial services.

Even with the carve-outs, litigation over where 'restraint of trade' ends and legitimate data sharing begins could take years to resolve, and enforcement costs would fall partly on insurers and their policyholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: consumers could gain from more competitive insurance pricing, while the industry gives up a shield against the most serious antitrust violations. The bill is narrowly written — it targets price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, not ordinary rate-setting — which limits the risk of unintended harm, though disputes over the boundary of the carve-outs would likely require courts to sort out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Insurance Competitive Pricing Act of 1993 on January 21, 1993, joined by Sens. Kennedy, Biden, and Simon.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, which was the last action recorded on it.
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers are better off: the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption remains intact, so price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization in insurance remain shielded from federal antitrust suits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The insurance industry, which kept its exemption

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the status quo under the McCarran-Ferguson Act and had a strong interest in keeping the bill bottled up; its lobbying against ending the antitrust exemption is a well-known feature of these recurring efforts.

sides.party_line_note: All four senators attached to the bill were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are recorded, and the bill never advanced to a vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would remove their federal antitrust shield for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, exposing coordinated conduct to federal lawsuits. Because insurers charge ordinary households and businesses for coverage, prices sustained by coordinated conduct come directly out of consumers' pockets.

The bill explicitly retains the antitrust exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, determining loss development factors, and actuarial services, keeping those cooperative structures intact and legal.
